screens.title: Comments: When to Use Them, When to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: In professional codebases, comments are a double-edged sword. They can clarify intent, but more often they rot out of sync with code and become misleading. In this lesson you will learn the clean-code stance: prefer self-documenting code first—meaningful names, small focused functions, and clear structure—and use comments only for facts the code cannot show. We'll look at concrete before-and-after code examples, practical rules for when a comment is appropriate, and a short hands-on refactor activity. You will see how renaming a function can remove the need for a comment, and when a short 'why' comment saves future debugging time. By the end, you should be able to spot redundant, misleading, and compensating comments, refactor code to reduce them, and write the limited, high-value comments that remain. Think of comments as scarce signals: keep them accurate, concise, and justified. As you move through the examples, ask yourself whether a comment explains intent that the code cannot, or whether a small refactor would make the comment unnecessary. That question is the key to cleaner, safer code.

screens.title: Why comments often cause harm
screens.narratorSegment: A comment becomes harmful when it diverges from the code it describes. Over time, teams modify code for new requirements or bug fixes, and comments are rarely updated with the same rigor. The result is a comment that asserts an outdated behavior or intent, which misdirects a reader and increases the chance of introducing a bug. A misleading comment is worse than silence because it actively encourages the wrong mental model. Let's define a misleading comment: it is a comment inconsistent with current code due to changes that were not reflected in prose. A redundant comment is one that simply repeats what the code already states in plain language, for example, a comment that says 'increment i' above a line that increments a loop counter. These do not add information and add maintenance cost. To make this concrete, imagine a function refactored to use a more efficient algorithm, but its comment still describes the old quadratic approach. A future maintainer reading the comment may attempt fixes based on the obsolete description, wasting time or introducing regressions. A useful exercise is to scan a function and ask: does this comment explain why something unusual is done, or does it restate the how? If it's the latter, refactor the code or remove the comment. The takeaway: treat comments as provisional and prefer naming and structure that reduce the need for them.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why comments often cause harm
Comments can become outdated or state the obvious. Learn to spot misleading and redundant comments.
Definition: Misleading comment
A comment inconsistent with current code because it was not updated.
Definition: Redundant comment
A comment that restates what code already shows, adding noise not value.
Key Takeaway

Prefer refactorings that remove the conditions that made the comment necessary; if a comment remains, make it concise and explain the rationale.

Concrete Example
# Bad comment example that becomes misleading after refactor
# Previously: used nested loops, now optimized to single pass
for item in items:
  process(item)

# The comment above still claims nested loops were used.
Misconception: People assume comments are safer than code. In reality, code is executable truth; comments are static text that can lie. Always ask whether the comment explains a rationale not visible in code, or if the code can be renamed or split to remove the comment entirely.
Check
When you see a comment, try to refactor instead of editing prose.
Question
Does this comment explain "why" or repeat "what"?

screens.title: Principles of Self-Documenting Code
screens.narratorSegment: Self-documenting code reduces the need for comments by making the program's intent explicit. There are three core practices to achieve this. First, choose meaningful names. A name should communicate purpose and intention, for example process_order rather than proc. Good names reduce the cognitive load on a reader and often eliminate the obvious comments. Second, extract small functions and classes. If a block of logic needs a comment to explain what it does, consider extracting it into a well-named function. Small, single-purpose functions read like a sentence and are easier to test. Third, organize code with clear structure: group related logic, use blank lines to separate concepts, and keep consistent formatting. This practice makes the control flow and data flow easier to follow. A concrete example: a five-line function with a descriptive name rarely benefits from an explanatory comment. Contrast this with a large function that mixes responsibilities; splitting it into two functions with clear names often removes the need for surrounding comments. A common misconception is that long comments are a substitute for design. They are not. Design and naming are the durable artifacts that survive refactors; comments must be updated manually. As a rule of thumb, prefer code changes to prose changes.

keyIdea.text: Meaningful names, small functions, and clear structure are the main levers to make code self-explanatory.

content.html:
Process Flow
Principles of Self-Documenting Code
Use naming, decomposition, and structure so the code communicates intent.
1. Meaningful Names
Names should reveal intent. Prefer process_order(data, amount) over proc(d,a).
2. Small Functions & Classes
Extract single-responsibility functions that read like verbs and nouns.
3. Clear Structure
Group related operations, use whitespace, and maintain consistent order of methods.
Key Takeaway

When a comment seems necessary to explain behavior, try renaming or extracting code first; only then consider a concise rationale comment.

Concrete Examples
Naming Example
Rename proc to process_order and d to data; the function's name explains the purpose without extra prose.
Extraction Example
If a block computes discount logic, extract apply_discount and test it independently instead of commenting the block.
Common Misconception
Comments are a substitute for poor naming. Instead, improve names and structure. If the code still needs a comment, it should explain why, not what.

screens.title: Refactoring an example: calc_total → Order
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a concrete refactor shown in the chapter. The original function initializes a total, loops through items adding their price, computes a discount, and returns a final total, all with comments that merely restate each line. The refactor creates an Order class, extracts calculate_subtotal and apply_discount methods, and uses descriptive variable names like subtotal and discount_amount. This change accomplishes several goals: it groups related data and behavior, provides clear method names that express intent, and leverages built-in functions to reduce ceremony. You will notice that the refactored code requires no explanatory comments because the method names and structure communicate the behavior directly. A misconception to avoid is thinking that classes always add unnecessary overhead; here, the Order abstraction models domain behavior and improves readability. For a guided exercise, take the original function, identify repeated responsibilities, extract them into named functions, and then rename variables to reflect domain terms. After the refactor, run the same unit tests to ensure behavior remains identical. Your final check: can a colleague read the new code and understand intent without referring to comments?

keyIdea.title: Refactor goal
keyIdea.text: Extract domain methods and prefer names that remove the need for descriptive comments.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Bad → Refactored
Compare the noisy commented function with the Order class that documents intent via names and small methods.
Bad Example (noisy comments)
def calc_total(items, discount_percent):
    # Initialize total to zero
    total = 0
    # Loop through each item
    for item in items:
        # Add item price to total
        total += item.price
    # Calculate discount amount
    discount_amount = total * (discount_percent / 100)
    # Subtract discount from total
    final_total = total - discount_amount
    # Return final calculated total
    return final_total
Refactored Version
class Order:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items

    def calculate_subtotal(self):
        return sum(item.price for item in self.items)

    def apply_discount(self, discount_percentage):
        subtotal = self.calculate_subtotal()
        discount_amount = subtotal * (discount_percentage / 100)
        return subtotal - discount_amount

# Usage:
# order = Order([Item(10), Item(20)])
# final_price = order.apply_discount(10)
The refactor groups related behavior, gives clear method names, and uses built-in operations, eliminating the need for line-by-line comments. Run tests to confirm behavior is invariant.

screens.title: When comments ARE appropriate
screens.narratorSegment: Despite the preference for self-documenting code, some comments are valuable and necessary. Use comments to explain the rationale behind an unusual decision that cannot be expressed by a name or a refactor. For example, a short comment may note a workaround for a third-party library bug with a bug ID or version number so future maintainers understand the reason for the atypical code. Legal information such as copyright headers or licensing metadata belongs in comments at the top of files. Warnings and TODOs that alert future developers to concurrency issues or incomplete refactors are legitimate, but they should be temporary and actionable. Public A P I documentation—docstrings or Javadoc—is not a substitute for internal comments; instead, it forms a contract for external users, documenting parameters, return values, and expected behavior. Finally, complex algorithms or mathematical formulas that underpin the implementation often need a short explanation of the theory, references, or equations to bridge domain knowledge gaps. A useful guideline: if the comment documents an invariant, reference, or why that cannot be derived from code, keep it. Otherwise, prefer refactorings. Always keep such comments concise and maintained alongside code changes.

content.html:
Definition
When comments are appropriate
Short, factual, and maintained comments that explain non-obvious rationale or legal requirements.
Explain the Why
Workarounds, versioned bug notes, or rationale for a trade-off.
Legal & Metadata
Licenses and copyright headers belong in comments at the file top.
Warnings & TODOs
Temporary alerts about thread-safety, deprecations, or unfinished work.
Docstrings / API docs
Public interfaces need clear formal documentation for consumers.
Concrete Example
# Workaround for Bug #12345 in external_library_v1.2
# The library mishandles empty lists; pass a dummy element as a temporary fix
if not data_list:
    data_list = [DUMMY_ELEMENT]
external_library.process(data_list)
This comment names the external bug and explains why the code deviates from the expected pattern. It is concise and actionable for future removal once the dependency is fixed.
Key Takeaway

Only keep comments that add non-derivable facts or contracts; remove everything else and improve the code instead.

screens.title: Refactor the age-group function
screens.narratorSegment: In this activity you will refactor a function that computes an age category from a birth year. The starter code includes comments that simply restate the code: comments that say 'Get current year' or 'Calculate age' add no value. Start by renaming the function and variables to clarify intent, for example change get_age_group to determine_age_group and current_year to now. Next, simplify conditionals: use clear range tests and prefer inclusive boundaries where they match domain language. If the logic benefits, extract a helper like is_teenager or categorize_age to encapsulate intent. Finally, if an assumption remains non-obvious — for example, whether the boundary includes or excludes the birthday day — add a concise 'why' comment explaining the choice. After refactoring, run the provided test cases to confirm behavior. A common misconception is that removing comments equals losing documentation; instead, you are transferring documentation into code constructs and tests that are executed and validated. The goal is to reduce prose and increase explicit, testable behavior. Refactor the age-group function means remove redundant comments by renaming functions and extracting helpers; keep only concise rationale comments when needed.. In practical terms, practice removing redundant comments and improving clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practice refactor
keyIdea.text: Remove redundant comments by renaming functions and extracting helpers; keep only concise rationale comments when needed.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Refactor get_age_group
Remove redundant comments, choose descriptive names, and extract helpers when helpful.
Starter Code
import datetime

def get_age_group(birth_year):
    # Get current year
    current_year = datetime.datetime.now().year
    # Calculate age
    age = current_year - birth_year

    # Determine age group based on age
    if age < 13:
        # Child category
        category = "Child"
    elif age >= 13 and age <= 19:
        # Teenager category
        category = "Teenager"
    elif age > 19 and age <= 64:
        # Adult category
        category = "Adult"
    else:
        # Senior category
        category = "Senior"
    # Return the determined category
    return category
Refactor Guidance
  • Rename to determine_age_group and variables to meaningful names like now and age.
  • Replace chained conditionals with clear ranges or helper functions such as is_child, is_teen.
  • Remove comments that restate code; add a short why-comment only if an assumption is non-obvious.
  • Include unit tests that assert expected categories for sample birth years.
Expected Refactor Example
def determine_age_group(birth_year, now=None):
    now = now or datetime.datetime.now().year
    age = now - birth_year

    if age < 13:
        return "Child"
    if 13 <= age <= 19:
        return "Teenager"
    if 20 <= age <= 64:
        return "Adult"
    return "Senior"

screens.title: Redundant vs. Helpful comments
screens.narratorSegment: When reviewing code, you will encounter many comments. Classify them quickly into three buckets: redundant, misleading, or helpful. Redundant comments restate the code; they add no new information and should usually be removed. Misleading comments contradict current behavior and should be corrected or deleted because they erode trust. Helpful comments add essential, non-derivable information such as the rationale behind an unusual decision, references to external bugs, or the mathematical derivation used in an algorithm. A practical review technique is to ask two questions for each comment: does the code already show this fact, and could renaming or extraction make the comment unnecessary? If both answers are yes, prefer refactoring. If the comment documents an invariant or a cross-file protocol that cannot be derived from local code, keep it but make it specific and succinct. For public APIs prefer docstrings instead of inline comments because docstrings are consumable by tools and signal a contract. Finally, when you keep a comment, add a short maintenance note: a TODO with tracker ID or a clear expiration condition. This helps ensure comments don't become stale.

keyIdea.title: Classification
keyIdea.text: Sort comments into redundant, misleading, or helpful. Prefer refactorings over prose; reserve comments for non-derivable facts.

content.html:
Comparison
Redundant vs Helpful Comments
A practical checklist to use during reviews.
Redundant
Restates the code, e.g., 'increment i' above i += 1. Remove after refactor.
Misleading
Describes behavior that no longer matches implementation. Fix or remove immediately.
Helpful
Explains rationale, external bugs, or complex math with references. Keep concise and maintained.
Review Checklist
  1. Can the code be renamed to make this comment unnecessary?
  2. Can the logic be extracted into a descriptive function or class?
  3. If the comment stays, does it explain why, include references, and set a maintenance action?
  4. For public APIs, move explanatory text to docstrings rather than inline comments.
Key Takeaway

Use a quick checklist in code review to reduce comment noise and preserve only high-value notes that explain the why.

screens.title: Design patterns that reduce comments
screens.narratorSegment: Design choices can remove the need for comments by making behavior explicit. Two patterns are especially effective. First, encapsulate domain concepts in small classes or modules. When the concept is encoded in the type system — for example an Order, Cart, or PriceCalculator class — the code itself documents responsibilities. Second, comprehensive tests act as living documentation: well-named unit tests describe behavior and boundary cases that comments might otherwise try to capture. Tests also ensure that changes do not silently invalidate assumptions described in comments. Use clear method names, expressive arguments, and return types where possible to communicate intent. Another helpful practice is to keep public interface docstrings up to date and include brief examples. A common misconception is that tests replace all documentation; they do not replace rationale comments for unusual decisions, but they do reduce the need for comments that only restate behavior. The practical step: when you find a comment explaining expected behavior, consider whether a focused unit test would better communicate and enforce that expectation. Design patterns that reduce comments means encapsulation and tests convert informal comments into durable, executable documentation.. In practical terms, small architectures and test suites as living documentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Common pitfalls and misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Developers commonly fall into a few traps when using comments. First, they use comments as a shortcut for poor naming—writing a long explanatory comment instead of choosing a clearer function or variable name. Second, comments are used to explain complex logic that actually needs decomposition into smaller, testable pieces. Third, teams accumulate TODOs and warnings without a plan to address them; these comments linger and clutter the code. Fourth, people assume comments are immutable documentation and skip updating them during refactors. To correct these habits, pair refactors with tests and code review: require that any lingering comment include an explicit ticket or expiration, and prefer small, named functions for complexity. A useful mental model is to treat comments as exceptional facts: they should be scarce, precise, and time-bound. When you educate a team, set a shared rule: if a comment explains 'what', remove it; if it explains 'why', keep it short and link to a tracker or external reference. This discipline reduces cognitive load and increases trust in the codebase. fullNarratorScript:
In professional codebases, comments are a double-edged sword. They can clarify intent, but more often they rot out of sync with code and become misleading. In this lesson you will learn the clean-code stance: prefer self-documenting code first—meaningful names, small focused functions, and clear structure—and use comments only for facts the code cannot show. We'll look at concrete before-and-after code examples, practical rules for when a comment is appropriate, and a short hands-on refactor activity. You will see how renaming a function can remove the need for a comment, and when a short 'why' comment saves future debugging time. By the end, you should be able to spot redundant, misleading, and compensating comments, refactor code to reduce them, and write the limited, high-value comments that remain. Think of comments as scarce signals: keep them accurate, concise, and justified. As you move through the examples, ask yourself whether a comment explains intent that the code cannot, or whether a small refactor would make the comment unnecessary. That question is the key to cleaner, safer code.

By the end of this lesson you will understand why the clean-code approach prefers self-documenting code over explanatory comments. First, you'll be able to identify code smells where comments compensate for unclear code and learn to spot redundant or misleading comments that increase maintenance risk. Second, you'll practice concrete techniques for self-documenting code: choosing descriptive names, extracting small functions, and organizing logic with clear structure. Third, you'll recognize the legitimate, limited reasons to keep comments: explaining the why behind unusual decisions, adding legal or licensing headers, and briefly noting TODOs or warnings that need follow-up. Finally, you will refactor a real example function to remove unnecessary comments while keeping only high-value explanatory notes. Each objective links to hands-on practice so you can apply these skills directly during code reviews and refactoring sessions.

This second objective slide focuses on practice and assessment. You will refactor a real function that is overloaded with redundant comments, applying naming and extraction to make the code self-explanatory. During the hands-on activity you'll remove comments that simply restate code, introduce descriptive function and variable names, and, when needed, add a concise 'why' comment for any remaining non-obvious logic. You'll also learn how to write useful docstrings for public interfaces where external users rely on them. Finally, the assessment asks you to point out at least two bad-comment patterns in a sample snippet and present a small refactor that removes them. Success means your refactor reduces comment lines while preserving or improving clarity and correctness. This practice helps you build a pattern of questioning each comment: can I refactor instead, or is this comment the sole source of crucial rationale?

A comment becomes harmful when it diverges from the code it describes. Over time, teams modify code for new requirements or bug fixes, and comments are rarely updated with the same rigor. The result is a comment that asserts an outdated behavior or intent, which misdirects a reader and increases the chance of introducing a bug. A misleading comment is worse than silence because it actively encourages the wrong mental model. Let's define a misleading comment: it is a comment inconsistent with current code due to changes that were not reflected in prose. A redundant comment is one that simply repeats what the code already states in plain language, for example, a comment that says 'increment i' above a line that increments a loop counter. These do not add information and add maintenance cost. To make this concrete, imagine a function refactored to use a more efficient algorithm, but its comment still describes the old quadratic approach. A future maintainer reading the comment may attempt fixes based on the obsolete description, wasting time or introducing regressions. A useful exercise is to scan a function and ask: does this comment explain why something unusual is done, or does it restate the how? If it's the latter, refactor the code or remove the comment. The takeaway: treat comments as provisional and prefer naming and structure that reduce the need for them.

Self-documenting code reduces the need for comments by making the program's intent explicit. There are three core practices to achieve this. First, choose meaningful names. A name should communicate purpose and intention, for example process_order rather than proc. Good names reduce the cognitive load on a reader and often eliminate the obvious comments. Second, extract small functions and classes. If a block of logic needs a comment to explain what it does, consider extracting it into a well-named function. Small, single-purpose functions read like a sentence and are easier to test. Third, organize code with clear structure: group related logic, use blank lines to separate concepts, and keep consistent formatting. This practice makes the control flow and data flow easier to follow. A concrete example: a five-line function with a descriptive name rarely benefits from an explanatory comment. Contrast this with a large function that mixes responsibilities; splitting it into two functions with clear names often removes the need for surrounding comments. A common misconception is that long comments are a substitute for design. They are not. Design and naming are the durable artifacts that survive refactors; comments must be updated manually. As a rule of thumb, prefer code changes to prose changes.

We'll walk through a concrete refactor shown in the chapter. The original function initializes a total, loops through items adding their price, computes a discount, and returns a final total, all with comments that merely restate each line. The refactor creates an Order class, extracts calculate_subtotal and apply_discount methods, and uses descriptive variable names like subtotal and discount_amount. This change accomplishes several goals: it groups related data and behavior, provides clear method names that express intent, and leverages built-in functions to reduce ceremony. You will notice that the refactored code requires no explanatory comments because the method names and structure communicate the behavior directly. Public A P I documentation—docstrings or Javadoc—is not a substitute for internal comments; instead, it forms a contract for external users, documenting parameters, return values, and expected behavior. Always keep such comments concise and maintained alongside code changes.
